items.stem:
Read the following extract from a playscript about a school talent show.

Backstage. Dim light. PRIYA paces, muttering lines. JAKE sits on an amp, eating crisps.
PRIYA: What if I forget the words? What if my voice cracks? What if everyone laughs?
JAKE: (crunching) What if you're brilliant?
PRIYA: (stops pacing) That's... not helpful.
JAKE: (standing, serious for once) Priya. You sang in the lift on the way here. Three people clapped. One was the lift man.
(Offstage, a voice calls: 'Priya Shah!' PRIYA freezes. JAKE gives her a thumbs up. She walks into the light.)

Which word best describes the overall tone of the text?
items.answer: comic and encouraging
items.markingKey: B. The tone is comic and encouraging: Jake's jokes ease Priya's nerves and lead to an uplifting end.

items.stem: Briefly explain why it is important to analyse structure as well as language.
items.answer: Structure (order, shifts, endings) shapes how meaning unfolds and how readers feel, so ignoring it misses half of the writer's choices.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Structure (order, shifts, endings) shapes how meaning unfolds and how readers feel, so ignoring it misses half of the writer's choices. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following leaflet from a school eco-club in Singapore.

GO PLASTIC-FREE THIS JULY!
Did you know? Our canteen throws away about 900 plastic cups every week. That's over 30,000 a year – enough to reach the top of Marina Bay Sands if you stacked them!
What can YOU do?
• Bring a reusable bottle (free refills at the new water fountains).
• Say "no straw, please".
• Join our Thursday lunchtime clean-up.
Small changes. Big difference. Sign up at the eco-club table by Friday!

What does "reusable" suggest here? Explain the connotations of the word in context.
items.answer: "reusable" means able to be used again here; it contrasts with single-use plastic and presents a practical solution.
items.markingKey: "reusable" means able to be used again here; it contrasts with single-use plastic and presents a practical solution. 1 mark for the meaning in context; further marks for connotation and effect.

items.stem: Write three annotations you would make on the opening of the attic extract: one on language, one on structure and one on effect.
items.answer: E.g. language: rhetorical question draws reader in; structure: slow climb up the stairs delays discovery; effect: reader shares Leila's fear and curiosity.
items.markingKey: E.g. language: rhetorical question draws reader in; structure: slow climb up the stairs delays discovery; effect: reader shares Leila's fear and curiosity.

items.stem:
Read the following free verse poem by a student poet, "Lagos at Midnight".

The city does not sleep;
it hums,
a generator heart
beating under every street.
Danfo buses honk like geese.
A radio somewhere
is singing to nobody,
and the moon,
tired of competing,
hides behind the billboards.

Unseen analysis. How does the poet use imagery and sound to present Lagos at night? Write about 300 words, using evidence and explaining effects on the reader.
items.answer: The extended metaphor "a generator heart / beating" presents the city as a living body. Onomatopoeia ("hums", "honk") and the comic simile "like geese" recreate the noise. Free-verse line breaks isolate sounds, and personification of the moon "tired of competing" shows the city's overwhelming light, while the radio "singing to nobody" adds a hint of loneliness.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The extended metaphor "a generator heart / beating" presents the city as a living body. Onomatopoeia ("hums", "honk") and the comic simile "like geese" recreate the noise. Free-verse line breaks isolate sounds, and personification of the moon "tired of competing" shows the city's overwhelming light, while the radio "singing to nobody" adds a hint of loneliness. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Feature-spotting (listing techniques) earns high marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: High marks require explaining the effects of choices and linking them to the writer's purpose, with evidence.
items.markingKey: High marks require explaining the effects of choices and linking them to the writer's purpose, with evidence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from a health website for teenagers.

[Headline in large white letters on dark blue: ARE YOU RUNNING ON EMPTY?]
[Icon of a phone battery at 20%: Teenagers need 8–10 hours of sleep a night.]
[Bar chart: 7 in 10 teenagers get less than 8 hours on school nights.]
[Three icons in a row: a moon, a closed book, a phone with a cross through it – "Same bedtime. Wind down. Screens off 1 hour before bed."]
[Small print: Source: national adolescent health survey, 2023.]

Unseen text analysis. How does the infographic use visual and verbal features to communicate its message quickly? Refer to language, layout or structure, and the intended audience.
items.answer: The rhetorical-question headline and the "running on empty" metaphor hook teenagers. The low-battery icon visualises tiredness in a familiar way, the bar chart proves the problem is widespread, and three simple icons with imperatives give memorable solutions; the source adds credibility.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The rhetorical-question headline and the "running on empty" metaphor hook teenagers. The low-battery icon visualises tiredness in a familiar way, the bar chart proves the problem is widespread, and three simple icons with imperatives give memorable solutions; the source adds credibility. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem: "Analysing an unseen text is harder than analysing a studied text." Discuss.
items.answer: It is more demanding under time pressure, but strong analytical skills transfer to any text; practice reduces the difficulty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: no prior knowledge or notes; time pressure. Arguments against: fresh reading can be more personal; the same skills apply. Supported judgement: It is more demanding under time pressure, but strong analytical skills transfer to any text; practice reduces the difficulty. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "annotation".
items.answer: Notes and highlights on a text identifying features and their effects
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: notes and highlights on a text identifying features and their effects. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a suspense story.

The attic door had been locked for as long as Leila could remember. 'Nothing up there but dust,' Gran always said.
So why, tonight, was there a light under it?
Leila climbed the stairs. Each step creaked. Each creak sounded like a warning.
She reached for the handle. It was warm.
Behind the door, something was humming – a tune she knew. The tune her mother used to sing.
Her mother had been gone for six years.

How does the one-sentence final paragraph shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The one-sentence final paragraph: isolating the revelation gives it maximum impact and creates a cliffhanger.
items.markingKey: The one-sentence final paragraph: isolating the revelation gives it maximum impact and creates a cliffhanger. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following short biography of the athlete Jesse Owens.

Jesse Owens was born in Alabama in 1913, the grandson of enslaved people. His family moved north to Ohio, where a school coach noticed how fast he ran.
In 1936 the Olympic Games were held in Berlin. Germany's Nazi government wanted the Games to show that its idea of racial superiority was true.
Owens won four gold medals – in the 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay.
Yet when he returned to the United States, he still faced segregation. 'I wasn't invited to shake hands with the President,' he later said.

In which four events did Owens win gold medals in 1936?
items.answer: The 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay.
items.markingKey: The 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An image used as a starting point for creative writing"?
items.answer: visual prompt
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of visual prompt.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an imaginative response to an image and a literal response to an image.
items.answer: A literal response simply describes what the image shows; an imaginative response uses the image as a springboard for a story, character or idea that goes beyond it.
items.markingKey: A literal response simply describes what the image shows; an imaginative response uses the image as a springboard for a story, character or idea that goes beyond it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why a clear structure matters in a 400–600 word piece.
items.answer: Limited space means every section must build towards a turning point and ending; a clear arc keeps the piece focused (criterion B). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Limited space means every section must build towards a turning point and ending; a clear arc keeps the piece focused (criterion B). (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Look at this image: a cracked smartphone screen lit up in the dark, showing 47 unread messages. Write three possible story ideas, each from a different perspective.
items.answer: Any three distinct ideas with perspectives (e.g. first person – a teen whose secret has been leaked; second person – "you" deciding whether to reply; third person – a parent finding the phone).
items.markingKey: Any three distinct ideas with perspectives (e.g. first person – a teen whose secret has been leaked; second person – "you" deciding whether to reply; third person – a parent finding the phone).

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a flooded street in a coastal town; a dog sits on the roof of a floating car, looking at the camera.]

Write the opening paragraph (about 150 words) of a story inspired by this image. Hook the reader and establish the mood.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a tense but strangely calm mood; possible idea – a rescue told by a volunteer, the dog's owner searching for it, or the day the river came; techniques such as present tense for immediacy, sensory detail of water, a powerful final image; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a tense but strangely calm mood; possible idea – a rescue told by a volunteer, the dog's owner searching for it, or the day the river came; techniques such as present tense for immediacy, sensory detail of water, a powerful final image; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a flooded street in a coastal town; a dog sits on the roof of a floating car, looking at the camera.]
Image 2: [A painting: a lighthouse on a black rock in a storm; its beam cuts across the waves towards a small boat.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a moving van parked outside a block of flats at dawn; a child presses a hand against the van's back window.]

Choose ONE image. Describe the mood it creates and suggest two different story ideas it could inspire, explaining whose perspective you would tell each from.
items.answer: Image 1: mood – tense but strangely calm; ideas – a rescue told by a volunteer, the dog's owner searching for it, or the day the river came | Image 2: mood – dramatic and hopeful; ideas – a keeper guiding a boat home, a rescue told from the boat, or a lighthouse that is about to be switched off forever | Image 3: mood – sad and reflective; ideas – leaving home, a friend left behind, or the first morning in a new country
items.markingKey: Indicative content (any image): Image 1: mood – tense but strangely calm; ideas – a rescue told by a volunteer, the dog's owner searching for it, or the day the river came | Image 2: mood – dramatic and hopeful; ideas – a keeper guiding a boat home, a rescue told from the boat, or a lighthouse that is about to be switched off forever | Image 3: mood – sad and reflective; ideas – leaving home, a friend left behind, or the first morning in a new country Marks: mood identified and justified from details (2); two plausible ideas (2); perspective explained (1).

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A painting: a lighthouse on a black rock in a storm; its beam cuts across the waves towards a small boat.]
Image 2: [A photograph: an abandoned greenhouse in Iceland, its glass broken, with tomatoes still growing wild inside.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a single lit window in a tall dark tower block at midnight; a silhouette is holding a sign against the glass that says "HELLO?".]

Choose ONE image and plan a creative piece of 400-600 words. State your form and audience, your narrator, a three-part structure and two language techniques you will use, with a reason for each.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: diary entry; narrator: a first-person narrator; structure: the storm builds – the boat is seen – the outcome at dawn; techniques: personification of the sea, light and dark imagery, a cyclical ending. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: diary entry; narrator: a first-person narrator; structure: the storm builds – the boat is seen – the outcome at dawn; techniques: personification of the sea, light and dark imagery, a cyclical ending. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a single lit window in a tall dark tower block at midnight; a silhouette is holding a sign against the glass that says "HELLO?".]
Image 2: [A photograph: two hands, one old and one young, holding the same chess piece above a board in a park in Moscow.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a girl in a football kit stands alone in a stadium tunnel, looking towards the bright pitch.]

Choose ONE image and use it as the starting point for a piece of imaginative writing (400-600 words). Give your piece a title.
items.answer: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a call for help, a game between neighbours, or loneliness in a big city; a first-person neighbour narrator; structure: noticing the sign – replying – meeting the person; techniques such as suspense, an epistolary element (signs as messages), a gentle twist. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image.
items.markingKey: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a call for help, a game between neighbours, or loneliness in a big city; a first-person neighbour narrator; structure: noticing the sign – replying – meeting the person; techniques such as suspense, an epistolary element (signs as messages), a gentle twist. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem: Briefly explain why choosing an unusual perspective can improve a creative piece.
items.answer: It makes a familiar image fresh and shows insight and imagination (criterion C).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It makes a familiar image fresh and shows insight and imagination (criterion C). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A creative piece must have a happy ending." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Endings should fit the story; open, bittersweet or surprising endings can be more powerful.
items.markingKey: Endings should fit the story; open, bittersweet or surprising endings can be more powerful. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "It is better to write a story than a diary entry or letter in response to a visual prompt." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Any form can succeed if it suits the idea and shows control; the best choice is the one that lets the writer show insight and style.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stories allow plot and character development; examiners expect narrative. Arguments against: diaries and letters can be intimate and original; any form can show creativity. Supported judgement: Any form can succeed if it suits the idea and shows control; the best choice is the one that lets the writer show insight and style. Markbands (12 marks): MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). A Analysing: explains content, context, language, structure, technique and style and their effects; justifies opinions with examples and explanation, using terminology. B Organising: a clear, logical structure suited to the task; ideas linked with purpose; referencing conventions. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited.

items.stem: What is the best use of the last five minutes of a timed writing task?
items.answer: Proofreading for errors and clarity
items.markingKey: A. Proofreading improves criterion D.

items.stem: "If your ideas are good, spelling and punctuation do not affect your mark." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Criterion D (Using language) assesses accuracy, so frequent errors lower the mark even when ideas are strong.
items.markingKey: Criterion D (Using language) assesses accuracy, so frequent errors lower the mark even when ideas are strong. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between proofreading and editing.
items.answer: Editing changes content, organisation and style to improve a draft; proofreading checks for surface errors such as spelling, punctuation and grammar.
items.markingKey: Editing changes content, organisation and style to improve a draft; proofreading checks for surface errors such as spelling, punctuation and grammar. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student's paragraph is mostly retelling the plot. Give two pieces of advice to improve it against criterion A.
items.answer: E.g. start with an analytical point about the writer's choice; embed a short quotation and explain its effect on the reader rather than what happens.
items.markingKey: E.g. start with an analytical point about the writer's choice; embed a short quotation and explain its effect on the reader rather than what happens.

items.stem: Find and correct the errors in this sentence (criterion D): "I could of won the race if I would of trained harder"
items.answer: I could have won the race if I had trained harder.
items.markingKey: I could have won the race if I had trained harder. Errors: "could of" → "could have"; "would of trained" → "had trained" (correct conditional); missing full stop. 1 mark per error corrected (max 4).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Self-assessment against the criteria is as useful as teacher feedback."
items.answer: Self-assessment is valuable when combined with teacher feedback; together they build understanding of the criteria.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it develops independence; students understand what is required. Arguments against: students may misjudge their work; teachers notice patterns students miss. Supported judgement: Self-assessment is valuable when combined with teacher feedback; together they build understanding of the criteria.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "drafting".
items.answer: Writing a first version, focusing on ideas and structure
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: writing a first version, focusing on ideas and structure. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Proofread and correct this passage: "I could of won the race if I would of trained harder"
items.answer: I could have won the race if I had trained harder.
items.markingKey: I could have won the race if I had trained harder. Errors: "could of" → "could have"; "would of trained" → "had trained" (correct conditional); missing full stop. 1 mark per error corrected (max 4).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "annotation"?
options: Notes and highlights on a text identifying features and their effects
A checklist of what a good response must include, often based on the assessment criteria
Writing a first version, focusing on ideas and structure
Improving a draft's content, structure and style, not just correcting errors
items.answer: Notes and highlights on a text identifying features and their effects
items.markingKey: A. "annotation" is notes and highlights on a text identifying features and their effects.

items.stem: What is the most effective way to use a visual prompt?
options: Use it as a starting point and develop an original idea beyond the literal image
Write about how the photo was taken
Describe every object in the image in order
items.answer: Use it as a starting point and develop an original idea beyond the literal image
items.markingKey: A. Examiners reward imaginative interpretation.

items.stem: Explain why planning saves time in a timed task.
items.answer: A plan sets out structure and key points in advance, so writing flows logically and the writer does not run out of ideas or time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A plan sets out structure and key points in advance, so writing flows logically and the writer does not run out of ideas or time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between structure analysis and language analysis.
items.answer: Language analysis looks at word-level and sentence-level choices (imagery, word choice, sentence types); structure analysis looks at how the whole text is organised (openings, shifts, pacing, endings).
items.markingKey: Language analysis looks at word-level and sentence-level choices (imagery, word choice, sentence types); structure analysis looks at how the whole text is organised (openings, shifts, pacing, endings). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why editing is different from proofreading.
items.answer: Editing improves ideas, structure and style (criteria B and C); proofreading corrects surface errors (criterion D). Both are needed.

items.stem:
Read the following travel blog post by a 15-year-old visiting Iceland.

Day 4: I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)
Posted by @nadia_explores
OK, so technically the eruption at Fagradalsfjall had stopped. But the ground was still breathing. Steam curled out of black rock like the earth was exhaling after a long run.
Our guide, Sigga, said the lava field was younger than me. I didn't know rocks could be younger than me!!
My boots smelled of sulphur (rotten eggs, basically) for two days. Worth it.
Drop a 🌋 in the comments if Iceland is on your list!

Rewrite the blog post as a short section (about 150 words) of a formal travel guide for families visiting Fagradalsfjall.
items.answer: Indicative content: third-person or impersonal voice; factual information (location, guided tours, safety around steam and gas, smell of sulphur); no emoji or slang; clear, formal register.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: third-person or impersonal voice; factual information (location, guided tours, safety around steam and gas, smell of sulphur); no emoji or slang; clear, formal register. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).

items.stem: When analysing an unseen extract, what should you do first?
options: Look only at the last line
Read the question and the whole extract carefully
items.answer: Read the question and the whole extract carefully
items.markingKey: B. Understanding comes before analysis.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "show, don't tell".
items.answer: Revealing emotions and ideas through specific details, actions and senses rather than stating them
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: revealing emotions and ideas through specific details, actions and senses rather than stating them. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between editing and proofreading.
items.answer: Editing changes content, organisation and style to improve a draft; proofreading checks for surface errors such as spelling, punctuation and grammar.
items.markingKey: Editing changes content, organisation and style to improve a draft; proofreading checks for surface errors such as spelling, punctuation and grammar. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following sequence of three haiku, "Monsoon Morning".

First fat drops of rain –
the dusty street holds its breath,
then the whole sky falls.

Children in puddles
splash the grey world into gold –
school bags overhead.

Evening. Frogs begin
their loud green orchestra; the
drains sing all night long.

Explain how the 5-7-5 syllable pattern of each haiku contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The 5-7-5 syllable pattern of each haiku: the strict, short form captures single moments, like snapshots.
items.markingKey: The 5-7-5 syllable pattern of each haiku: the strict, short form captures single moments, like snapshots. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature or technique, a precise quotation or reference, and an explanation of its effect on the reader linked to the writer's purpose (criterion A). Naming a feature without explaining its effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Distinguish between second-person narration and first-person narration.
items.answer: First person ("I") lets the reader share one character's thoughts; second person ("you") places the reader inside the story, which can feel immediate and unsettling.
items.markingKey: First person ("I") lets the reader share one character's thoughts; second person ("you") places the reader inside the story, which can feel immediate and unsettling. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "If your ideas are good, spelling and punctuation do not affect your mark." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Criterion D (Using language) assesses accuracy, so frequent errors lower the mark even when ideas are strong.
items.markingKey: Criterion D (Using language) assesses accuracy, so frequent errors lower the mark even when ideas are strong. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a first-person novel about two friends.

Dev and I built the treehouse the summer we were ten. We nailed a sign to it: NO GROWN-UPS. NO GIRLS. NO EXCEPTIONS.
Now we're thirteen and the sign is still there, faded and crooked, and Dev hasn't climbed up for months.
Today I saw him at the bus stop with Marcus's crowd. He laughed at something Marcus said. I waved. He looked at his shoes.
I went home and climbed the ladder alone. I took the sign down. Then I put it back up. I don't know why.

Explain what the word "crooked" means in this text and why the writer chose it.
items.answer: "crooked" means not straight; bent or twisted here; it suggests the friendship is now damaged and out of shape.
items.markingKey: "crooked" means not straight; bent or twisted here; it suggests the friendship is now damaged and out of shape. 1 mark for the meaning in context; further marks for connotation and effect.

items.stem:
Look at the image described below.

[A photograph: a schoolbag left on a bench at a bus stop in heavy rain; the bus's red tail-lights disappear around the corner.]

Write a descriptive paragraph (about 150 words) that recreates this scene using at least three senses.
items.answer: Indicative content: establishes a frustrated and lonely mood; possible idea – a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs; a hook that raises a question.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: establishes a frustrated and lonely mood; possible idea – a missed bus that changes a day, a forgotten bag that holds a secret, or a moment of rebellion; techniques such as pathetic fallacy, a twist, short paragraphs; a hook that raises a question. Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from a short story set in Cape Town.

The poster had been on the lamppost for three weeks: MISSING – BRUNO – REWARD. The rain had washed the dog's face into a grey smudge.
Thabo passed it every morning. Every morning he told himself it wasn't his business.
Then, on Thursday, behind the fish shop, something whined.
It was thin, and it was muddy, and one ear stood up like a question mark.
Thabo crouched. The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward. He thought about his mother's empty purse.
"Come on, Bruno," he whispered. "Let's get you home."

Unseen analysis. How does the writer build tension around Thabo's decision? Write about 300 words, using evidence and explaining effects on the reader.
items.answer: Repetition ("Every morning he told himself...") establishes his avoidance, so the shift "Then, on Thursday" signals change. Short, parallel sentences ("The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward.") slow the pace as he weighs his options, and the detail of the "empty purse" raises the stakes. The whispered ending resolves the tension with kindness while leaving his motives ambiguous.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Repetition ("Every morning he told himself...") establishes his avoidance, so the shift "Then, on Thursday" signals change. Short, parallel sentences ("The dog looked at him. He looked at the poster. He looked at the reward.") slow the pace as he weighs his options, and the detail of the "empty purse" raises the stakes. The whispered ending resolves the tension with kindness while leaving his motives ambiguous. Mark mainly against criterion A (Analysing) and B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: perceptive analysis of how specific choices create effects, well-chosen embedded evidence, sustained, logical structure; 5-6: substantial analysis with relevant evidence; 3-4: adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2: limited, mostly feature-spotting or retelling.

items.stem:
Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: snow falling on a market in Kraków; a stallholder pours hot chocolate for a girl who is counting coins.]
Image 2: [A painting: a wide golden wheatfield with a single tree; a red kite is caught in its branches.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a cracked mirror propped against a wall in an empty room; it reflects a doorway, but the doorway is not in the room.]

Choose ONE image and plan a creative piece of 400-600 words. State your form and audience, your narrator, a three-part structure and two language techniques you will use, with a reason for each.
items.answer: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the cold – the coins don't add up – the kindness; techniques: sensory contrast of cold and warmth, dialogue, understatement. Plans for the other images must show the same elements.
items.markingKey: Model plan for Image 1 – form: story; narrator: a third-person narrator; structure: the cold – the coins don't add up – the kindness; techniques: sensory contrast of cold and warmth, dialogue, understatement. Plans for the other images must show the same elements. Marks: form and audience (1); narrator and perspective (1); coherent structure with a turning point (2); purposeful techniques (1).

items.stem: Find and correct the errors in this sentence (criterion D): "Yesterday me and my freind goes to the beach. We seen a dolphin, it was amazing."
items.answer: Yesterday my friend and I went to the beach. We saw a dolphin; it was amazing.
items.markingKey: Yesterday my friend and I went to the beach. We saw a dolphin; it was amazing. Errors: "me and my freind" → "my friend and I" (subject pronoun, spelling); "goes" → "went" (tense); "seen" → "saw"; comma splice → semicolon or full stop. 1 mark per error corrected (max 4).

items.stem:
Read the following travel blog post by a 15-year-old visiting Iceland.

Day 4: I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)
Posted by @nadia_explores
OK, so technically the eruption at Fagradalsfjall had stopped. But the ground was still breathing. Steam curled out of black rock like the earth was exhaling after a long run.
Our guide, Sigga, said the lava field was younger than me. I didn't know rocks could be younger than me!!
My boots smelled of sulphur (rotten eggs, basically) for two days. Worth it.
Drop a 🌋 in the comments if Iceland is on your list!

Unseen text analysis. How does the blogger make her experience vivid and entertaining for her readers? Refer to language, layout or structure, and the intended audience.
items.answer: Personification and simile ("the ground was still breathing", "like the earth was exhaling") make the volcano feel alive. Humour – the bracketed "(and Lived)", "(rotten eggs, basically)" – and exclamation marks create a chatty, friendly voice, while the comment invitation and emoji draw readers into a community.

Look at the three images described below.

Image 1: [A photograph: a girl in a football kit stands alone in a stadium tunnel, looking towards the bright pitch.]
Image 2: [A drawing: a city where all the buildings are made of books; a boy reads on a balcony while pages flutter down like snow.]
Image 3: [A photograph: a cracked smartphone screen lit up in the dark, showing 47 unread messages.]

Choose ONE image and use it as the starting point for a piece of imaginative writing (400-600 words). Give your piece a title.
items.answer: Indicative content (Image 1 example): a first match after an injury, a trial for a national team, or proving a doubter wrong; a first-person narrator; structure: doubt in the tunnel – flashback to training – stepping into the light; techniques such as internal monologue, light and dark contrast, a ticking clock. Any image and form may be chosen; the piece should go beyond literal description of the image.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student council president to her school assembly in Toronto.

Good morning, everyone. Raise your hand if you checked your phone before breakfast today. (Pause.) Me too.
We are the most connected generation in history – and, according to our own school survey, 62 per cent of us say we feel lonely every week. Connected, but alone.
I'm not asking you to throw your phone in the lake. I'm asking for one hour. One lunchtime a week, phones in our bags, eyes on each other.
Let's try it. Let's talk. Let's remember what our friends' faces look like when they laugh.

Write a response to the speech for the school newspaper (about 200 words), giving your opinion on the phone-free lunchtime idea.
items.answer: Indicative content: headline; clear opinion; reference to the speaker's points (statistic, "Connected, but alone"); one counterargument (e.g. phones help some students feel included); conclusion.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: headline; clear opinion; reference to the speaker's points (statistic, "Connected, but alone"); one counterargument (e.g. phones help some students feel included); conclusion. Indicative content above. Mark against criteria B, C and D: purpose and audience addressed (C), conventions of the form and logical organisation (B), register, vocabulary and accuracy (D).
